rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis's claim that he was superior because he came from fire while Adam came from clay makes lineage a Satanic basis for superiority; God's measure is obedience.
rows.anchor: the philosophy of regarding one’s lineage to be a basis of superiority is an invention of Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deliberate disobedience is arrogance: it treats oneself as superior or equal to God, whose exaltedness alone is fitting; the arrogant are humiliated and excluded from Paradise.
rows.anchor: deliberate rebellion from God’s directive is arrogance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise belongs to those who humble themselves before and worship God; Iblis's arrogance earned expulsion and lasting humiliation.
rows.anchor: Paradise is only a place for those who humble themselves before God and worship Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an names arrogance as the actual barrier to Paradise in its camel analogy, while Jesus' comparison cites wealth, a frequent source of arrogance.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān has referred to the actual sin: arrogance and Jesus (sws) has referred to wealth which generally becomes the source of arrogance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human life becomes a trial in which Satan tries to discredit human worth while people must prove their fitness for Paradise; the final verdict comes on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: Satan spends all his efforts in planning to prove human beings to be unworthy and failed creatures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The respite lets Satan tempt people until death, when their record closes; his request to wait until Judgment Day delays the decision on human dignity.
rows.anchor: Since his request was granted, it means that he was able to delay the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan frames God as his real adversary, making the conflict one between himself and God rather than between himself and human beings.
rows.anchor: He regarded God be his actual enemy and that is why he challenged him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By saying God led him astray, Satan claims he was right to refuse Adam's prostration and blames God for placing him in a test he could not pass.
rows.anchor: the words “since you have led me astray” show that he regarded himself to be on the right path when he refused to prostrate before Adam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human nature is directly connected to God and, absent unnatural distortion, a person can follow only monotheism.
rows.anchor: a person cannot adopt any path but the path of monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Monotheism is the straight path: even slow progress reaches its destination, whereas turning toward polytheism leads farther astray.
rows.anchor: As long as a person keeps treading this path, he walks towards his destination

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan can fully mislead someone only by diverting them from monotheism to polytheism, so he announces an ambush on the path of monotheism.
rows.anchor: Satan is not able to lead a person astray totally unless he is able to divert him from the wide path of monotheism to the narrow path of polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attacks from every direction picture Satan's comprehensive assault on human perception, emotion, desire, thought, research, art, culture, society, economics, politics, and religion.
rows.anchor: They are an expression of the power, extent and comprehensive nature of Satan’s onslaught from his own tongue.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge is repeated in Sūrah Banī Isrā’īl, where Satan's broad propaganda includes political tactics aimed at carrying out his mission.
rows.anchor: This very challenge of Satan is cited in verses 62-65 of S ūrah Banī Isrā’īl thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's propaganda is extensive, but he cannot override human will; people retain freedom to choose, and God's servants can remain monotheists despite his schemes and danger.
rows.anchor: The latter will have the freedom of will to choose their way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling most people ungrateful means that most are not monotheists, since true monotheism recognizes God's favors and thanks Him.
rows.anchor: “and You will find most of them not to be monotheists.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attributing God's favors to anyone else amounts to polytheism; the issue was discussed earlier and will receive further attention in the sūrah.
rows.anchor: If he attributed these favours to anyone other than God, then this would be tantamount to polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the next part of Adam and Satan's story; its purpose was treated in Sūrah al-Baqarah, while this passage explains points not covered there.
rows.anchor: These verses narrate the next part of the anecdote of Adam (sws) and Satan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam and Eve could eat from anything in Paradise, with the single forbidden tree serving as their trial.
rows.anchor: They were just stopped from going near one tree and it was this tree that became a trial for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan lured Adam with the forbidden tree's supposed benefits, using the same tactic on his descendants by presenting a few prohibited things as the secret of success.
rows.anchor: Everything of this world is permissible for them except a few things. It is these few things that Satan and his accomplices use to lure them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The granted respite left Satan free to reach Adam and Eve, and he used it to whisper his enticing suggestion.
rows.anchor: It is evident from this respite that there was no hindrance for Satan to reach Adam (sws) and Eve.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām marks consequence: Satan sought to prompt disobedience and ingratitude, which appeared in Adam and Eve's loss of Paradise clothing.
rows.anchor: is for consequence. Satan wanted to entice Adam (sws) to show disobedience and ingratitude to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Losing their robes meant Adam and Eve now had to meet their needs through their own efforts, whereas God had previously arranged everything.
rows.anchor: now Adam (sws) will have to provide for his needs through his efforts.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's claim that the tree was forbidden lest they become angels or immortal shows Adam regarded angels as higher and knew his life was not eternal.
rows.anchor: Your Lord has only stopped you from this tree lest you become angels or that you may acquire immortality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form qāsama normally suggests sharing but can intensify an action; here it conveys Satan's repeated oaths to establish credibility with Adam and Eve.
rows.anchor: it is only used to signify multiplicity and exaggeration. Thus it is evident from this verb that Satan had to make a great effort to create his credibility.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom fadalāhumā means Satan deceived the pair in whatever way he wished.
rows.anchor: he deceived him in whatever way he wanted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasting the tree means tasting its fruit; Arabic commonly suppresses the governing noun, muḍāf.
rows.anchor: Tasting the tree means to taste the fruit of the tree. It is common to suppress the governing noun (muḍāf) in Arabic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb khṣafa means to join or fasten; after violating the command, Adam and Eve lost their Paradise attire and covered themselves with leaves.
rows.anchor: The verb ﺧﺼﻒmeans “to join and to fasten.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their exposed nakedness depicts the shame of sudden loss of clothing, while covering themselves with leaves shows their timidity and bewilderment.
rows.anchor: the words “their private parts became evident to them.” After them, the words “and they began covering themselves with leaves of the garden” depict the timidity and bewilderment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The urge to cover one's private parts is natural, as are modesty and monotheism; shamelessness and polytheism are artificially adopted.
rows.anchor: the feeling of hiding one’s private parts is a natural instinct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's rebuke recalls the earlier warnings about the tree, Satan's enmity, and the fate of those who follow him.
rows.anchor: refer to the warnings mentioned in verses 17 to 19. The nature of enmity of Satan with Adam (sws) had also been explained

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam and Eve's confession is repentance after God rebuked them for breaking their promise; it is treated more fully in Sūrah al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: This repentance has been referred to in S ūrah al-Baqarah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam's repentance, unlike Iblis's arrogant response, won back a lost round, was accepted by God, and exemplifies the way his descendants should respond after Satan's lure.
rows.anchor: Through this repentance Adam (sws) won a round that he had lost. It has already been mentioned about Iblīs that in spite of the rebuke, he became arrogant
